summary: Defines the Extensible Binary Meta Language (EBML), a binary container format designed for audio and video storage, like a binary counterpart to XML. It uses nested elements with identifiers, lengths and values, and describes EBML Schemas, similar to XML Schemas. Matroska builds on it.

plainLanguage.summary: EBML is a way of storing data in a file so that a reader can find each part without reading the whole file. Every piece of data is written as a label, a length and the value itself, and the pieces can be nested inside one another. The structure is fixed by this RFC, while the meaning of each label is set by a separate schema, in the same way XML separates structure from meaning.

questions: what file formats are built on ebml
what is a variable-size integer in ebml
how does ebml relate to matroska
subtitle: A compact binary format for nested, self-describing data, built to store audio and video.

tldr.problem: Multimedia container formats need a generic, space-efficient, easy-to-parse way to nest data, with structure kept separate from meaning.
tldr.mechanism: Every EBML Element is an Element ID, an Element Data Size and Element Data. IDs and sizes are variable-size integers that say their own length, and an EBML Schema defines which elements a document type may contain.
tldr.outcome: EBML is the structural layer used by the Matroska container. The RFC defines the header, element types, versioning, CRC-32 and Void elements, and IANA registries. A later RFC updates it.

facts.label: Default max Element Data Size length

today: RFC 8794 is a Proposed Standard. It has been updated by RFC 9559, and it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
EBML, short for Extensible Binary Meta Language, specifies a binary format aligned to octets and inspired by the principle of XML, which is a framework for structuring data.

The goal is a generic, binary, space-efficient format that can be used to define more complex formats using an EBML Schema. EBML is used by the multimedia container Matroska; the applicability of EBML to other use cases is beyond the scope of the document.

The format recognizes the idea behind HTML and XML as a good one: separate structure and semantics, so that the same structural layer can carry very different semantic layers. Except for the EBML Header and a few global elements, the document does not define particular EBML format semantics. It defines how other EBML-based formats can be defined, such as the Matroska and WebM container formats.

EBML builds every element on three pieces of data: a tag, a length and a value. This approach is well known, easy to parse and allows selective parsing, so a reader can skip over data it does not need. The structure also allows a hierarchical arrangement, which supports complex formats efficiently.

A typical EBML file has this shape: an EBML Header holding the DocType and the DocTypeVersion, and an EBML Body Root holding elements, some of which are themselves containers of further elements.
sections.plainLanguage: EBML is a binary container format, and it is the structural layer under formats such as Matroska. It separates the shape of the data from its meaning: this RFC fixes the shape, and a schema fixes the meaning. Every item in the file carries its own length, so a reader can walk straight to the part it wants.

sections.title: The Variable-Size Integer
sections.content:
The Element ID and the Element Data Size are both encoded as a Variable-Size Integer, also called a VINT. A VINT is composed of a VINT_WIDTH, a VINT_MARKER and the VINT_DATA, in that order, and the value must be left-padded with zero bits so that the whole integer is octet aligned.

The VINT_WIDTH is a sequence of zero or more zero bits terminated by the VINT_MARKER, a single bit of value one. The total length in bits of the width and the marker is the total length in octets of the integer: a single one bit starts a one-octet integer, the bits 01 start a two-octet integer, 001 start a three-octet integer, and each additional zero adds one octet.

The VINT_DATA is everything after the marker. The width and the marker use one bit out of every eight, so a one-octet integer leaves 7 bits for data, a two-octet integer leaves 14 bits, a three-octet integer leaves 21 bits, a four-octet integer leaves 28 bits and a five-octet integer leaves 35 bits. If the value needs fewer bits than are available, the data must be zero-padded on the left, and the value is expressed as a big-endian unsigned integer.

An integer may be written at a longer octet length than it needs, so that it can be overwritten later with a longer value, for example when its final size is not known in advance. The value 2 has the same meaning whether it is written as 0x82 in one octet, 0x4002 in two, 0x200002 in three or 0x10000002 in four.
sections.plainLanguage: A number that says how long it is. The first one bit in the number marks the end of the length prefix, so a reader can tell from the first byte how many bytes the number uses. The number then carries one bit less per byte than the bytes it occupies, and it is stored most significant byte first. Writing the same value in more bytes than needed is allowed, which lets a writer leave room to change it later.

sections.title: The Element ID and the Element Data Size
sections.content:
An Element ID is a Variable-Size Integer that uniquely identifies a defined EBML Element within a specific EBML Schema. By default, Element IDs are from one octet to four octets in length, although longer ones may be used if the EBMLMaxIDLength element of the EBML Header says so. The bits of the VINT_DATA of an Element ID must not be all zeros or all ones, and the VINT_DATA must be encoded at the shortest valid length. The binary encoding 1011 1111 is therefore a valid Element ID, while 0100 0000 0011 1111 stores the same value but is invalid because a shorter encoding exists. The encoding 1111 1111 is invalid because the data is all ones, while 0100 0000 0111 1111 stores a semantically equal value in the shortest possible encoding.

The range and the count of possible Element IDs follow from their octet length. A one-octet Element ID ranges from 0x81 to 0xFE, which gives 126 valid IDs. A two-octet Element ID ranges from 0x407F to 0x7FFE, giving 16,256. A three-octet Element ID ranges from 0x203FFF to 0x3FFFFE, giving 2,080,768. A four-octet Element ID ranges from 0x101FFFFF to 0x1FFFFFFE, giving 268,338,304.

The Element Data Size expresses the length in octets of the Element Data and is itself encoded as a Variable-Size Integer. By default it is from one octet to eight octets long, and longer ones may be used if the EBMLMaxSizeLength element of the EBML Header declares them. Unlike the data of an Element ID, the value of an Element Data Size is not required to be encoded at the shortest valid length, so 1011 1111 and 0100 0000 0011 1111 are both valid and both store the value 63.

An Element Data Size with all data bits set to zero means the Element Data is zero octets long, which makes the element an Empty Element. If the element has a default value, the reader must use that default; if it has none, the reader must use the zero value for the type, which is 0 for numbers and an empty string for strings. An Element Data Size with all data bits set to one is reserved as the indicator that the size is unknown. Only a Master Element may have an unknown size, and only when the unknownsizeallowed attribute of its schema is set to true. The end of an unknown-sized element is decided by whichever comes first: an element that is a valid parent of it, a valid element that is not a descendant but shares a direct parent, a valid root element, the end of the parent element with a known size, or the end of the document.

An Element Data Size of eight octets can express a size of 2^(56)-2 octets, about 72 petabytes. If the length of the Element Data equals 2^(n*7)-1, the octet length of the Element Data Size must be at least n+1, so that a real length is never mistaken for the unknown-size value.
sections.plainLanguage: Every element starts with a label and a length, both written as variable-size integers. The label must not use a reserved code and must be written in the shortest form that fits, so a one-byte label leaves room for 126 labels and a two-byte label for 16,256. The length field has two reserved values: all zero bits means the value is empty, and all one bits means the length is not known yet, which is only allowed for a container element whose schema permits it. The length field may be written in more bytes than it needs, which is what makes later editing possible.

sections.title: The Element Types
sections.content:
An EBML Schema must declare one of the following element types for each element. A type defines how the data is stored, including its length, its endianness and its meaning. Elements defined as a signed integer, an unsigned integer, a float or a date use big-endian storage.

  • A signed integer declares a length from zero to eight octets and is stored in two's complement with the leftmost bit as the sign bit, so it holds a number from -9,223,372,036,854,775,808 to +9,223,372,036,854,775,807. With no default value, a zero-octet length means the value zero.
  • An unsigned integer declares a length from zero to eight octets and holds a number from 0 to 18,446,744,073,709,551,615, with zero for a zero-octet length when there is no default.
  • A float declares a length of zero, four or eight octets and stores a number in the 32-bit or 64-bit binary interchange format of IEEE 754.
  • A string declares a length from zero to VINTMAX and holds printable ASCII characters in the range 0x20 to 0x7E, with an exception for termination.
  • A UTF-8 element declares a length from zero to VINTMAX and holds a valid Unicode string, again with an exception for termination.
  • A date declares a length of zero or eight octets and stores nanoseconds from 2001-01-01T00:00:00.000000000 UTC, which covers 1708-09-11T00:12:44.854775808 UTC to 2293-04-11T11:47:16.854775807 UTC.
  • A master element declares a length from zero to VINTMAX or is of unknown length, and contains zero or more other elements. Data inside it that is not part of a child element must be ignored.
  • A binary element declares a length from zero to VINTMAX, and its contents should not be interpreted by the reader.
sections.plainLanguage: The schema says what each element holds: a whole number, a number with a fraction, text in ASCII or in Unicode, a timestamp, a container of other elements, or bytes that are left alone. Numbers and timestamps are stored most significant byte first, and the largest integer an element can hold is about 18,446,744,073,709,551,615.

sections.title: Documents, Headers and Bodies
sections.content:
An EBML Document is composed of only two components, the EBML Header and the EBML Body, and it must start with a header. It must not contain any data that is not part of an element.

The EBML Header is a declaration that gives processing instructions and identifies the body, and it is analogous to the XML declaration of an XML document. It names the EBML Schema, also called the DocType, that is used to interpret the document, and it records the versions of both EBML and the schema that were used to write the document and the versions required to read it. The header must contain a single master element with the name EBML and the Element ID 0x1A45DFA3, which is reserved for the header and for resynchronization. Elements inside the header can be at most four octets long, except the EBML element itself, which can be up to eight octets long.

All data after the header is the EBML Body. The body ends when a new EBML Header appears at the root level or when the file ends, whichever comes first. The header sets the maximum length allowed for an Element ID and for an Element Data Size in the body.

An EBML Stream is a file made of one or more EBML Documents concatenated together, and an occurrence of a header at the root level marks the start of a document.

A document handles two versions. The version of the header is in EBMLVersion, and a parser can read the header if it can read that version or a version equal to or higher than the one in EBMLReadVersion. The version of the body is in DocTypeVersion, and a parser for that DocType can read the document if it can read that version or one equal to or higher than the one in DocTypeReadVersion. Both versions are meant to be backward compatible.
sections.plainLanguage: Every file starts with a header that says what the file is and which version of the format it uses, and then comes the body with the actual data. The header has a reserved label that readers use to find the start of a document, so a reader can resynchronize after damage. The version numbers let an old reader handle a file written by a newer version, as long as it can read the version the file asks for or a later one.

sections.title: The EBML Schema
sections.content:
An EBML Schema is a well-formed XML document that defines the properties, the arrangement and the usage of the elements that make up a particular EBML Document Type. The relationship between a schema and a document is analogous to the relationship between an XML Schema and an XML document. A schema must be clearly associated with one or more document types, and a document type is identified by a string stored in the DocType element of the header, for example Matroska or WebM. The DocType value must be unique, persistent and described in the IANA registry.

A schema must declare exactly one element at root level, the root element, which occurs exactly once in a document. The Void element may also occur at root level but is not a root element. The schema must document all the elements of the body, and it must not use the Element ID 0x1A45DFA3.

The schema is written in XML with the namespace urn:ietf:rfc:8794. The top-level element is EBMLSchema, and it carries a required docType attribute naming the document type and a required version attribute giving the version of that document type the schema documents. Unlike XML Schemas, one EBML Schema documents all the versions of a document type, and elements are introduced and deprecated with the minver and maxver attributes. Each element node gives the element a name, a path, an ID, a type and how often it may occur, and it may carry documentation, an implementation note, a restriction and extension elements.
sections.plainLanguage: The schema is a separate XML document that says which elements a given kind of EBML file may contain, what each one means and where it may appear. It names the document type, and it keeps the history of that type in one file, with the version in which each element appeared and the version in which it was dropped, rather than a separate schema per version.

sections.title: Reading and Updating EBML Data
sections.content:
When a master element holds a CRC-32 element that does not validate, the reader may ignore all the data it contains, except for descendant elements that carry their own valid CRC-32 element. If a master element contains more occurrences of a child master element than the maxOccurs attribute allows, the extra occurrences may be ignored. If it contains more occurrences of a child element than allowed, all instances after the first maxOccurs should be ignored.

Null octets, which are octets with all bits set to zero, may follow the value of a string or UTF-8 element as a terminator. A writer may use them to overwrite a stored value with a shorter one while keeping the same Element Data Size, which avoids rewriting large parts of the document. The element data must be a valid string up to the end of the element or the first null octet, whichever comes first, and the null octet and anything after it should be ignored.

An EBML document can be updated without rewriting it in full. When an element shrinks by more than one octet, the writer should fill the freed space with a Void Element. For a shrink of a single octet, the writer may instead rewrite the Element Data Size in a longer octet length, so the element keeps its overall length and the data around it does not move. Terminating the data with null octets is not recommended. If the element being changed sits inside a master element that carries a CRC-32 element, that CRC must be checked before the change is allowed and must then be updated.

For compatibility, a new element can be made mandatory while keeping old readers working, by giving it a default value that represents the state assumed by earlier versions of the schema; if such a state makes no sense, the element should not be mandatory. Non-mandatory elements can be added in a new DocType version without causing a compatibility problem. An element may be marked as deprecated with the maxver attribute, and if it turns up in a document of a newer version it should be discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: A reader that finds a checksum that does not match may throw away the data inside that container, but keeps the parts that carry their own valid checksum. A writer that wants to shorten a value does not have to move the rest of the file: it can leave the freed bytes as a Void element, or write the length field in more bytes than before, and for text it can end the value with a zero byte.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
EBML itself offers no kind of security and no confidentiality, and it provides no authorization. It offers only marginally useful data integrity options, such as the CRC elements.

Even if the semantic layer offers encryption, EBML could leak information at the semantic layer, through the DocType declared in the header, and within the structure itself, because the presence of elements can be derived even with an unknown semantic layer, using a heuristic approach that is not error free but reasonably confident.

A reader may discard some or all data when it finds an invalid Element ID longer than the limit in the header, an Element ID that is not encoded in the shortest possible way, an invalid Element Data Size longer than the limit in the header, an invalid data size such as one that extends past the end of the parent element, very high lengths that force an out-of-memory condition, missing elements that are mandatory and have no default value, invalid UTF-8 in a text element, invalid data in a date element, or a CRC-32 element that does not match the content of its master element.

Side-channel attacks could exploit the fact that a string and the same string padded with zero bits are semantically equal, that the same data size written at two different lengths is semantically equal, and that data inside a master element that is not part of a child element is ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: EBML itself does nothing to protect the data it carries. It has no encryption, no access control and only a weak checksum. Even if an application encrypts its content, the file still shows what format it is and which elements are present. A reader must also be careful with broken files, since a bad length field could claim more space than the file has, and a very large one could exhaust memory.
